objectives: Describe how a water heater can put current into the water, into the pipes and into a person.
Name current, voltage, insulation, earthing, leakage current and the residual-current device, and say what each one does.
Explain why a bathroom is the place where a small electrical fault becomes dangerous.
Separate the electrical protection from the pressure protection, so that the right part is checked.
Compare the protective earth wire, the residual-current device and the circuit breaker by what each one watches.
Use the right order of action when somebody gets a shock from a hot water appliance.
Check the label of a heater and the maintenance that stops the fault from happening.

sections.body:
A water heater is a metal tank that holds water, and an element inside it that heats the water with electricity. The element, the wiring and the water all live in the same metal case. That is why the appliance stands at the edge of two hazards: it holds hot water under pressure, and it carries mains current. The second one can stop a heart, and it is the one this article is about.

Five words carry the subject. **Electric current** is the flow of electricity, measured in amperes (A). **Voltage** is the push that drives the current, measured in volts (V); the supply to a house is usually around 230 V in much of the world and around 120 V in North America. **Insulation** is the material around the live part of the appliance that keeps the current inside the cable. The **earth wire**, called the ground wire in North America, is the green-and-yellow conductor that connects the metal case to the earth bar in the board, so that a fault current has a short way back. And water with minerals in it carries current: pure water is a poor conductor, but tap water is not pure water.

The fault is simple to state. If the live part of the heater touches the tank or the water, current can leave the cable, cross into the water, reach the pipes, and then reach the person who is holding a tap. Nothing about the heater looks wrong from outside. The fault is inside the case, and it is done to a person standing on a wet floor.

This article explains what the fault is, what the parts do, what to do in the first minutes, and when to stop and call a professional. It does not replace the manual of the appliance, and it does not replace the work of a licensed electrician.
examples: The heater is a metal tank with water and an element inside it, so the case is part of the circuit.
A fault current that reaches the water can reach the pipes, and the pipes can reach the person.
The manual and the electrician decide what is done; this article only explains the risk.
sections.heading: What the risk is: electricity inside a tank of water

sections.body:
Current does not travel alone. It needs a closed path: it leaves the board on the live wire and comes back on the neutral wire, and it will take any path that closes the loop. If the live part of the heater touches the water, the water becomes part of that loop. The pipes that carry the water become part of it too, and so does every tap and every metal fitting joined to them.

Your body joins the circuit the moment it touches two points at different voltages. While you stand on a wet floor and hold a metal tap, current passes through you instead of through the earth wire that was meant to carry it safely. Water on the skin lowers the resistance of the body, so more current passes, and the current that passes through the heart is the one that matters.

So the paths in a bathroom are worth naming: water in the pipes, a wet floor, a metal tap, a towel or a mat lying on the floor, and a heater whose case has lost its insulation. Any one of them on its own is harmless. A person, a floor and a pipe together are the fault.

The small amount of current that always finds its way through the insulation is called **leakage current**. In a healthy installation it is small and steady. When the insulation breaks down, the leakage current grows, and it is that growth, not the size of the fault, that usually warns you first: the residual-current device starts to trip.
examples: If the live part touches the water, the pipes become part of the circuit.
A wet floor and a metal tap make a path that a person can stand on without touching the heater.
The RCD was tripping because the leakage current had grown, not because the heater was overloaded.
sections.heading: How current finds a path to a person

terms.example: The electrician measured the leakage current and it was above the usual level.
terms.gloss: Current that escapes from the live part of the appliance through damaged insulation.

sections.body:
Three arrangements protect the person, and each one watches a different thing. The first is the **protective earth wire**, the green-and-yellow conductor that connects the metal case of the heater to the earth bar in the board. Its job is to give a fault current a low-resistance path back to the board, so that a large current appears on the circuit and the circuit breaker opens. It also keeps the metalwork of the pipework at a voltage near zero. **Earthing** is the whole arrangement of conductors and connections; the earth wire is one conductor inside it. **Bonding** is the part of that arrangement that joins metal parts to each other, such as pipes, the case of the heater and metal fittings, so that no single metal part can sit at a voltage that a person can touch.

The second arrangement is the **residual-current device** (RCD), also called RCB or RCCB. It compares the current that goes out on the live wire with the current that comes back on the neutral wire. In a healthy circuit the two are the same. When they differ, some current has gone somewhere else: through a person, through water, or through insulation that has failed. That difference is the residual current, and when the RCD sees it the device **trips**, opening the live and the neutral in a fraction of a second, long before the current can do serious harm. It does not know where the current went, and it does not need to. It knows only that some of it is missing.

The third arrangement is the insulation of the cable and the circuit breaker at the end of it. The insulation keeps the current inside the cable where it belongs, and the breaker watches the current against the rating of the cable and opens the circuit when it is too high. A breaker protects the cable and the appliance; on its own it does not protect a person from a small leakage current. That is the work of the RCD. A residual current of 30 mA is the usual level for personal protection in most installations, and the local standard decides.

All of that is about current. The pressure protection is a separate system. The **safety valve**, usually a temperature-and-pressure relief valve, opens if the pressure inside the tank rises too high and lets water out. The **anode rod** is not a valve at all: it is a rod of a metal that corrodes more easily than the steel tank, and it corrodes instead of the tank wall. A heater can have every one of these parts working perfectly and still put a person at risk if the earth wire has been cut. Read the two systems as two systems.
examples: The earth wire carries the fault current back to the board, and the breaker opens.
The RCD compares the current that goes out with the current that comes back.
The safety valve protects the tank from pressure, and the RCD protects the person from current.

sections.body:
Six parts do the work, and they belong to two different systems. The first three watch the electricity: the protective earth wire, the residual-current device and the circuit breaker. They protect the person. The last three watch heat, pressure and corrosion inside the tank: the relief valve, the anode rod and the thermal cut-out. They protect the appliance. A reader who mixes the two groups will wait for the wrong part to save them.

The thermal cut-out sits between the groups. It is a switch inside the tank that opens the heating circuit when the water is too hot, so it protects the element and the insulation around it. It does not protect a person from a fault to earth, and it does not make the water safe to touch.

The ratings in the table are the common levels, not the law. A residual current of 30 mA is the usual level for personal protection, a 16 A breaker is common for a socket circuit, and the water heater is often on a dedicated circuit of its own. The local standard decides every one of these values. If the installation in front of you does not match the table, ask the electrician or the utility what it should be.
examples: The earth wire and the RCD protect the person; the relief valve and the anode rod protect the tank.
A 16 A breaker on a socket circuit is common, and the local standard decides the value.
The RCD trips when the current that comes back is less than the current that went out.

sections.body:
A shock from a hot water appliance happens in a wet room, and the first minutes decide the result. The order below matters. Do not start with the person; start with the power. The rule that governs everything else: never touch a person who is still in contact with the water or the appliance. A person holding a tap, or standing in a puddle and holding a pipe, is still part of the circuit. Your hand on their arm makes you part of it as well.

Switch off the power at the breaker or the main switch if you can reach it without entering the wet area. If you cannot reach it safely, do not go into the water. Move everybody out of the room, call the emergency number and the utility, and wait for the power to be cut from a safe position. The wet floor around a live appliance is where the second casualty is made.

Then make the room safe. Dry the floor around the appliance and dry the person, especially the hands and the feet. Do not touch the light switch or the tap in the wet area: you cannot be sure that the earth path is working, and this is the moment not to test it.

Then call for help and write the day down. If the person is not responding, or if you are not sure how serious it is, call the emergency number in your country: 113 for police and traffic and 115 for an ambulance in Vietnam, 112 in much of Europe, 999 in the United Kingdom and 911 in the United States. Say where you are, what happened and what the person is doing now. After that, call the electrician or the utility, keep the heater out of service until it has been checked, and write down the time of the event, the symptoms and the names of the people you called.
examples: Do not touch her until the power is off; she is still standing in the water.
I have switched off the breaker and I am drying the floor now.
I am calling the emergency number because he is not responding.

sections.body:
**Never work on the heater with the power on.** Not the element, not the wiring, not the plug, and not with the breaker switched off and the hope that it was already off. If you cannot confirm that the circuit is dead, you do not work on it.

**Never reset the RCD again and again.** A device that trips has found a fault. Resetting it clears the evidence and puts the fault back. Note what the appliance was doing, note the time, and call the electrician. A device that trips twice in one week is a fault to be reported, not a nuisance to be pushed.

**Never use an extension cord or a portable heater in a wet room.** An extension lead is a long, poorly protected conductor, and a portable heater is a live element on the floor of a wet room. Neither belongs in a bathroom. If the socket is far from the appliance, the answer is a new circuit fitted by an electrician, not a lead across the room.

**Never rely on the earth wire alone.** The earth wire is one layer of protection, and it only works when the board sees the fault current. The RCD is the layer that watches the person. A heater with a good earth and no RCD protection is not safe, and a heater with a good RCD and a cut earth wire is not safe either. And one rule stands above the four: **only a licensed electrician opens, repairs or tests a water heater.** The manual of the appliance, the local standard and the certificate of the electrician decide what is done. This article explains what happens and what to do in the first minutes. It is not a repair instruction, and it does not replace any of those three.
examples: I will not reset the RCD again; it has tripped twice and the fault has to be found.
We do not use an extension lead for the heater; the socket is too far from the appliance.
Only a licensed electrician opens and tests the heater, so I will call one.
sections.heading: Four things never to do

sections.body:
Most of what you need in this trade is the language of a report. Say what you saw, say what the device did, and say what you want done next. Do not diagnose the fault yourself; describe the symptom and let the electrician decide the cause.

A technician needs four things: where the heater is, what the label says, the symptom in the order it happened, and what has already been tried. Read the label before you call, and keep it in front of you when the technician arrives.

A landlord or an office manager needs the same facts in a shorter form, plus the request: a date, a reference number and the statement that the appliance is out of service. A colleague needs the rule and the warning: switch off, call, do not reset.
examples: The RCD tripped twice yesterday evening, and the heater is now out of service.
The label gives the make and the model, and I have written them down.
Someone got a shock from the shower while the heater was running; I have switched off the power at the board.
Could you send a licensed electrician and give me a reference number for the visit?
The bathroom stays out of use until the earth connection has been checked.
I do not know what caused it; I can tell you exactly what I saw.
Do not reset the device. Call the utility and let them find the fault.
Is the routine service included in the lease, or do I have to arrange it?
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
Most faults inside a water heater begin as a slow change that nobody notices. Hard water carries minerals, and every time the heater runs, some of them settle on the element and inside the tank as scale. Scale is a thermal insulator: the element has to work harder for the same setting, it runs hotter, and the insulation around it ages faster. **Descaling** is the removal of that scale. It is a job for the maker's procedure, and in many cases for a professional. Do not put anything into the tank that the maker does not name.

The anode rod is the part that is meant to corrode. It is a rod of magnesium, or another metal that is more active than steel, screwed into the head of the tank, and while it is there the corrosion eats the rod instead of the tank wall. Check it at the service interval, and have it replaced when it is mostly gone. A tank that has lost its rod can fail from the inside with no warning at the tap.

At the same visit, flush the tank so that the sediment on the bottom goes out, and check that the drain valve opens and closes, because a valve that cannot be opened is a valve that cannot be used. Check that the relief valve is not stuck and that its discharge pipe is clear. With the power off, look at the cable and the plug for damage: a cut, a crushed section, a pin that is hot or discoloured, a plug that moves in the socket.

Set the temperature so that the water cannot **scald** a person. A storage temperature of about 60 °C is the usual recommendation in many installations, and the local code decides. Read the label of the heater before you change anything: it names the type of appliance, the rating, the range of the thermostat and the service intervals the maker expects. A label is not decoration.
examples: The heater needs descaling every year in this building, because the water is hard.
The anode rod is checked and replaced at the service, not when the tank starts to leak.
The label sets the range of the thermostat, and the local code decides the maximum temperature.
sections.heading: The maintenance that prevents the fault

terms.example: Water at 60 °C can scald a child in a few seconds.
terms.gloss: A burn caused by hot liquid or steam.

terms.example: Descaling is done at the service interval in hard water areas.
terms.gloss: Removing the mineral scale that builds up inside a tank and on the heating element.

item.summary: A water heater is a metal tank full of water with electricity inside it. After reading this article you can describe how a fault current reaches a person, name the parts that protect you, do the right things in the first minutes after a shock, describe the fault to a technician, and keep the appliance safe between services.
